problem:
Given a string s made only of the characters ()[]{}, decide whether the brackets are balanced: every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket, and brackets close in the correct order.

Example: s = "()[]{}" -> true
Example: s = "([)]" -> false
Example: s = "{[]}" -> true

data.key_insight: The last opened bracket must be the first one closed, which follows Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) order perfectly matched by a stack.

steps.title: Initialize a stack
steps.detail: Create an empty list to act as a stack for tracking opening brackets.

steps.title: Define bracket mappings
steps.detail: Create a dictionary mapping closing brackets to their corresponding opening brackets.

steps.title: Iterate through the string
steps.detail: For each character in the string, if it is a closing bracket, check if the stack is non-empty and the top element matches the expected opening bracket. If not, return false.

steps.title: Handle opening brackets
steps.detail: If it is an opening bracket, push it onto the stack.

steps.title: Final validation
steps.detail: After checking all characters, return true if the stack is empty, meaning all brackets were correctly closed.

data.pattern_summary: A stack is a Last-In, First-Out data structure used when elements must be processed in reverse order of their arrival, matching most recent openings with corresponding closings.

pattern_options.name: Stack
pattern_options.feedback: This fits because the most recently opened bracket must be closed first, matching LIFO behavior.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers work well for sorted arrays or palindromes, but bracket nesting requires tracking unclosed pairs across varying distances.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: A hash map helps store pairs like closing-to-opening brackets, but it does not maintain the order required to validate nested structures.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Sliding windows deal with contiguous subarrays or substrings of a fixed size, which does not apply to matching nested symbols.

signals.phrase: every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket
signals.hint: Implies a strict pairing rule between specific characters.

signals.phrase: brackets close in the correct order
signals.hint: Suggests that nested or sequential structures have precedence constraints based on arrival order.

data.brute_force_idea: Repeatedly find and remove adjacent valid pairs of brackets from the string until no more pairs can be removed, then check if the string is empty.
data.brute_force_why: Each pass through the string checks and replaces substrings, taking linear time, and we might need to repeat this process up to n/2 times.
data.bottleneck: The provided brute force solution already avoids major wasted work and runs efficiently in practice, though a single pass using a stack is cleaner and avoids string mutation overhead.
bottleneck_hints: Consider the order in which items are added and removed.
Think about which bracket needs to be checked against a closing bracket.
No faster approach is strictly necessary since linear time is already achieved by tracking state in order.

data.overview: The algorithm uses a stack to keep track of open brackets as it iterates through the string. When a closing bracket is encountered, it checks if it matches the most recently opened bracket on top of the stack.
data.intuition: Think of a stack of plates: you can only add or remove the plate on the very top. When closing brackets appear, they must match the most recently added opening plate.

flow_nodes.detail: Pop the top element from the stack (or use a dummy value if empty) and verify it matches the expected opening bracket.

flow_nodes.detail: If it is an opening bracket, push it onto the stack.

flow_nodes.detail: Return true if the stack is completely empty, meaning all brackets were properly closed.

data.insight: The brute force solution repeatedly scans and modifies the entire string for matching pairs, leading to redundant work. The optimized solution uses a stack to process each character once in a single pass. Opening brackets are pushed onto the stack, and closing brackets immediately check the top of the stack for their matching counterpart.

derivation.note: The for loop iterates over each of the n characters in the string.
Checking if the character exists in the mapping dictionary takes O(1) time per iteration.
Stack pop operations run in O(1) time whenever a closing bracket is encountered.
Stack append operations run in O(1) time whenever an opening bracket is encountered.

data.time_summary: Line 5 runs n times, executing constant-time checks on lines 6, 7, 8, and 11 on each iteration. The total operations scale linearly with n, resulting in O(n) time complexity, which is confirmed by the measured step growth.
data.space_summary: In the worst-case scenario where the string contains only opening brackets, the stack stores all n characters. This requires O(n) auxiliary space.
data.takeaway: When problems require matching nested structures or pairs in a specific order, use a stack to keep track of recent elements that await a counterpart.
mistakes: Forgetting to check if the stack is empty before popping, which raises an IndexError.
Failing to check if the stack is empty at the end of the loop, missing cases with unmatched trailing opening brackets.
Using string replacement loops that rescan the entire string repeatedly, resulting in worse time complexity.
